{{< include _compose-kit.qmd >}}

When you write for a real player, you need to know three things about their instrument. **Which notes it can play** (its range), **how its
part is written** (its clef, and whether it transposes), and **what is easy or hard** on it. This lesson covers the first two for the orchestra,
the saxophones and the guitar. The next lesson uses them to arrange.

## 1. The families

The orchestra is described in four families:

| Family | Instruments (high to low) | How the sound is made |
|---|---|---|
| **Woodwinds** | piccolo, flute, oboe, English horn, clarinet, bass clarinet, bassoon, contrabassoon | air across an edge (flutes), or a reed (one: clarinet, saxophone; two: oboe, bassoon) |
| **Brass** | trumpet, horn, trombone, tuba | the player's lips buzzing in a cup-shaped mouthpiece |
| **Percussion** | timpani, then everything struck, shaken or scraped; harp and piano are often placed nearby | striking |
| **Strings** | violin (in two sections, firsts and seconds), viola, cello, double bass | a bow drawn across the string, or plucking (*pizzicato*) |

Saxophones belong with the woodwinds (they have a single reed). They are not regular members of the orchestra, but some scores from the 19th century on use them.

## 2. Ranges

These are the **sounding** ranges: the notes the audience hears, with middle C as C4. The top notes are approximate: good players go higher,
and young players should usually stay well below them.

| Instrument | Lowest | Highest (about) | Clef |
|---|---|---|---|
| Violin | G3 | E7 | treble |
| Viola | C3 | C6 | alto |
| Cello | C2 | E5 | bass (tenor and treble for high notes) |
| Double bass | E1 | B3 | bass, written an octave higher |
| Flute | C4 | C7 | treble |
| Oboe | B♭3 | F6 | treble |
| English horn | E♭3 | B♭5 | treble, transposes |
| Clarinet in B♭ | D3 | B♭6 | treble, transposes |
| Bassoon | B♭1 | B♭5 | bass (tenor for high notes) |
| Horn in F | B1 | F5 | treble (bass for low notes), transposes |
| Trumpet in B♭ | E3 | B♭5 | treble, transposes |
| Trombone (tenor) | E2 | B♭4 | bass |
| Timpani | F2 | F4 | bass |
| Alto saxophone | D♭3 | A♭5 | treble, transposes |
| Tenor saxophone | A♭2 | E5 | treble, transposes |

<div class="cp-tip">
<strong>The middle is where it sounds best.</strong> The lowest notes of a flute are quiet and breathy; the highest notes of a trumpet are loud and
tiring. If a part has to be heard, put it where the instrument is strong, not where it only just reaches.
</div>

## 3. Transposing instruments

On a **transposing instrument** the written note is not the note that sounds. A clarinet in B♭ that reads C plays a B♭: everything sounds a
major second lower than written. So the clarinet's part has to be **written a major second higher** than the music should sound.

Why do it? So that one set of fingerings works for every size of the instrument. A player who learns the alto saxophone can pick up a tenor and
read the same written notes with the same fingers; the tenor just sounds lower. Instruments that sound an octave away from their written notes
(guitar, double bass, piccolo) are written that way to avoid a staff full of ledger lines.

**Concert pitch** is what the piano plays: the sounding note. A score "in C" shows every part at concert pitch; a *transposed score*
shows each part as its player reads it.

| Instrument | A written C sounds | So write the part |
|---|---|---|
| Clarinet in B♭, trumpet in B♭ | B♭, a major 2nd lower | a major 2nd higher |
| Horn in F, English horn | F, a perfect 5th lower | a perfect 5th higher |
| Alto saxophone (E♭) | E♭, a major 6th lower | a major 6th higher |
| Tenor saxophone (B♭) | B♭, a major 9th lower | a major 9th higher |
| Guitar, double bass | C, an octave lower | an octave higher |
| Piccolo | C, an octave higher | an octave lower |

The key signature moves too. Music in F for the band is in G for the clarinets and trumpets (one flat becomes one sharp), and in D for the
alto saxophones.

## 4. Try it: the transposer

Write the music as it should sound (in ABC, concert pitch), pick an instrument, and read the part its player would get. The check underneath says
whether every note is inside that instrument's range.

<div class="cp-try">
<div class="cp-transpose"></div>
</div>

Try putting the melody in the bass clef range (add `,` after the letters to move notes down an octave) and pick the cello, then the
trombone, then the alto saxophone. Notice which instruments can't reach it.

<div class="cp-tip">
<strong>Ask the player.</strong> The table gives the limits; a player can tell you what is comfortable at their level, which notes are awkward,
and how long they can play before they need a rest. Recording a player trying your part, and writing down what they said, is some of the best
evidence of developing a piece you can have (see [Process 1](process-journal.qmd)).
</div>
